How do I track changes to a public licence register?

Credentialing teams and specialist recruiters have the same recurring job: a public register of licences, permits or registrations matters to their work, and it changes without telling anyone. The usual method is to re-read the current export and hope something looks different from last quarter, which finds additions occasionally and removals almost never.

Comparing two dated exports finds all three kinds of change, and produces a record of having looked.

Open Public-Record Watch

What a comparison gives you that re-reading does not

  • Added records — entries present now that were absent before.
  • Removed records — the class a manual pass misses most, because nothing on the page draws attention to an absence.
  • Changed fields — a status, a category, an expiry date, or a name that moved on a record that stayed put.

Every record carries a stable id and the register's source URL, so each reported change points back at the original public entry rather than at a summary of it.

A removal is a question, not an answer. A record can leave an export because the export was filtered differently, because the register was partially unavailable when it was taken, because an identifier changed, or because of a routine administrative correction. Open the source record and confirm before acting.

The line this tool does not cross

It compares snapshots the customer is authorized to supply — each input must declare authorized: true, a register name, and a source URL. It does not scrape registers, build profiles of people, aggregate sources, rank or score anyone, decide suitability, or assert that a person is compliant, safe, or eligible. A public register entry is a fact about a record; it is not a judgement about a person, and a diff of two exports must not be used as one.

How to use it

  1. Take an authorized export of the register and keep it as a dated snapshot. Take the next one on your review cadence.
  2. Run the comparison over the before and after snapshots. It runs locally and offline — no account, API key, or hosted service.
  3. Read the report in Markdown or JSON, and open the source URL for anything you intend to act on.
  4. File the report with the date you reviewed it. That is the record that you looked.

Common questions

How do I track changes to a public licence register?

Export the register on a regular cadence, keep each export as a dated snapshot, and compare consecutive snapshots rather than re-reading the current one. A comparison gives you the three things a manual review does not reliably produce: the records that appeared, the records that disappeared, and the fields that changed on records that stayed. Keep the source URL with each record so a reviewer can open the original entry instead of trusting the summary.

Does a record disappearing mean a licence was revoked?

No, and treating it that way is the main risk in this workflow. A record can vanish from an export because the export was filtered differently, because the register was partially unavailable, because an identifier changed, or because of an ordinary administrative correction. A removal is an observation that tells you where to look. Open the source record and confirm before acting on it, and never let a diff become the basis of a decision about a person on its own.

Does this build profiles of people?

No. It compares two snapshots that you are authorized to supply and reports what differs between them. It does not scrape registers, aggregate sources into profiles, rank or score people, judge suitability, or state that anyone is compliant, safe, or eligible. Each input must be marked as authorized and must carry the register name and source URL, so every reported change points back at a public record a reviewer can read.

It reports differences between snapshots you supply, which may be incomplete or out of date. Verify every change against the original public record and take advice from a qualified professional before making any decision that affects a person. index.html.text:
Public-Record Watch

Did a public license, permit, or registration record change? Paste a dated before and after export of the register and get a source-linked review record — entirely in your browser.

Paste your two register exports as JSON (authorized, register, source_url, records):

Don't have exports handy? — a small before/after pair with an added, removed, and changed record, so you can see the report shape before using your own.

What this is and isn't

  • Everything runs in your browser. The exports you paste are never uploaded — there is no server here to send them to.
  • This tool never scrapes a register itself. You (or your own export process) supply both dated, customer-authorized snapshots; this only compares them.
  • It does not create personal profiles, rank people, decide suitability, or claim that a person is compliant, safe, or eligible — it reports added, removed, and changed records only. That judgment is yours.
  • Every record's source URL is carried into the report so a reviewer can open the original public record before acting.
  • Only anonymous, aggregate usage counts (for example "a comparison was run") may be recorded locally — never register names, record ids, or record fields.

Common questions

Does this fetch the register for me?

No. This tool never makes a network request to a register. You supply both snapshots — however you exported them — and this only compares the two. That keeps it usable for registers with no public API, a login wall, or a rate limit a general fetcher could never respect.

What counts as a valid snapshot?

A JSON object with authorized: true (you attest you're authorized to hold this export), a register name, a source_url the report links back to, and a records list where every record has a unique id. All other record fields are compared as-is.

Why doesn't a removed record mean the person lost their license?

A record missing from the "after" export could mean the license lapsed, the export was incomplete, or the register reorganized its ids. This tool reports the observation only; the reviewer opens the source URL and confirms what actually happened before relying on it.

Is my export uploaded anywhere?

No. Comparison happens with JavaScript running in your own browser tab. This page makes no network request with your pasted content — there is nothing to intercept because nothing is sent. Only anonymous, aggregate usage counts like "a comparison was run" may be recorded locally, with an opt-out below.

Is there a command-line version?

Yes — the same comparison logic ships as a local Python CLI (src/public_record_watch/cli.py) in this tool's repository, for scripted use. See the README for its usage.

vs-visualping.html.text:
← Public-Record Watch

This tool vs. Visualping

Visualping visits a URL for you on a schedule and reports what changed on the page. This tool never visits anything — you supply two dated, authorized register exports yourself, and it reports what changed between the records in them, source-linked back to the register.

What each tool is for

Visualping is a general-purpose website change monitor. Point it at a URL and a schedule, and it fetches the page for you, keeps a screenshot history, and produces a visual diff and plain-language summary of what moved, with alerts when it does. That is exactly the right tool for a public page a scheduled visitor can reach and render on its own — a pricing page, a job listing, a status page.

Many licence, permit, and registration registers are not that page. They sit behind a search form, a session, a CAPTCHA, or an "export" button rather than a single stable URL a crawler can revisit, and a scheduled visitor cannot fill those in for you. This tool assumes exactly that case: you export the register however your own access actually works, keep each export as a dated, authorized snapshot, and this tool compares two of them — reporting which record ids were added, which were removed, and which fields changed on records that stayed, each one still linked to the source URL so a reviewer can open the original entry. It runs free in your browser or as a local command-line tool, keeps no account, and makes no network request of its own; there is nothing here that visits a register on your behalf, so there is nothing to configure, pause, or explain to whoever administers that register's access.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I need a page watched automatically on a schedule, with screenshots and alerts.Visualping, or a comparable page-change monitor.
The register sits behind a search form, login, or export button — nothing a scheduled crawler could revisit on its own.This tool — you export it yourself, this tool only compares.
I need a per-record diff (added / removed / changed id) with a source link, not a screenshot.This tool's structured comparison report.
I want a record I can hand a credentialing or procurement reviewer, tracing straight back to the source register.This tool's source-linked output.
I need something scripted, offline, for a repeatable local workflow.This tool's command-line version.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?Neither tool requires one at the free tier.

The two do not compete so much as start from opposite assumptions about how you reach the source. Visualping assumes a URL a scheduled visitor can reach and render; this tool assumes you already have (or can produce) a dated export and just need the comparison and the source-linked record. For a register with a plain, stable, publicly fetchable page, a scheduled monitor like Visualping may be all you need. For a register you can only reach through a search form, a login, or a manual export, this tool is built for exactly that gap.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: comparison runs in your own browser or locally on the command line, and nothing you paste or export is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Should I use this tool or Visualping to track a public register?

It depends on how the register can be reached. Visualping is a general-purpose website change monitor: point it at a URL and a schedule, and it visits the page for you, takes a screenshot, and produces an AI summary and visual diff of what moved, with alerts. That is the right tool for a public page a scheduled visitor can reach and render cleanly on its own. Many licence, permit, and registration registers are not that page: they sit behind a search form, a session, a CAPTCHA, or an export button, and a scheduled visitor cannot fill those in for you. This tool assumes exactly that case. You export the register yourself, however your access actually works, keep each export as a dated snapshot, and this tool compares two of them and reports what was added, removed, or changed, with the source URL carried through to each record. Nothing here visits a register on your behalf, so there is nothing that can be blocked, rate-limited, or logged in as you without your knowledge.

Does this tool fetch or scrape the register for me, like Visualping does?

No, and that is the whole design. Visualping's job is to visit a URL automatically on a schedule so you do not have to. This tool never makes a network request to a register at all — you supply both snapshots, captured however your own export process works, and it only compares the two you give it. That makes it usable for registers with no stable public URL, a login wall, a CAPTCHA, or a rate limit that an automated visitor could not respect anyway; it also means there is no scheduled crawler running against a register on your behalf that you would need to configure, pause, or explain.

Do I lose the screenshot and AI summary Visualping gives me?

Yes, this tool does not attempt that, and for a register export it is the wrong shape of comparison. A visual screenshot diff is built for pages where layout and rendered content are what changed. A register export is structured data — rows with an id, a set of fields, and a source URL — and the useful comparison is per-record: which ids appeared, which disappeared, and which fields changed on records that stayed, each one still linked back to its source so a reviewer can open the original entry. That is a different report than a picture of two page renders, and it is the one this tool produces.

Is this page affiliated with Visualping?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Visualping or its operators. Visualping is named here only to describe what this tool is and is not, and no claim is made about it beyond its well-documented category: a website change detection and monitoring service that visits a URL on a schedule.

It only compares snapshots you are authorized to supply. A removed record may mean an export changed or a source was incomplete — inspect the source before acting. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.
